claims.claim: Cobb notes Crispin's surviving second mosaic is on a smaller scale and more obliquely expressed, the novel implying that is why it lasts.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings
claims.quote: on a smaller scale and more obliquely expressed

claims.claim: Cobb contrasts Kay's sense of proportion, the smallness of the human being in relation to the world, with Silverberg's hero who masters history.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings
claims.quote: the smallness of the human being in relation to the world

claims.claim: Töyrylä estimates about sixty per cent of Tigana is focalized through Devin or Dianora, with at least nineteen other identifiable focal characters and most chapters alternating three or more perspectives.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: About sixty per cent of the text

claims.claim: Töyrylä shows Dianora's passages use free indirect thought with the character's own metaphors, deictics and incomplete sentences, amplifying the emotional notes.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: incomplete sentences point in the direction of the character

claims.claim: Töyrylä points to the long list of verbs ('battered and levelled and burned... and killed... and taken away') as the character's voice inside the narration.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)

claims.claim: Töyrylä notes Alberico is a regular focal character, which humanises him with frustration and fear without making him sympathetic.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: Using the antagonist as a focal character makes him

claims.claim: Töyrylä analyses the Ring Dive as narrated twice or thrice through Devin, Dianora and Alessan, with contradictory readings of Brandin's expressionless face.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: some of the events are narrated twice or even thrice

claims.claim: Töyrylä shows Rhun is never a focal character until the final pages, enabling the Valentin twist while other focalizants register him in passing.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: the focalization unexpectedly shifts to him

claims.claim: Töyrylä reads the innkeeper Ettocio: focalized for a few pages, then a shift to narratorial focalization enables the matter-of-fact description of his execution.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: enables the matter-of-fact description of his execution

claims.claim: Töyrylä finds narratorial passages are matter-of-fact description with only minimal commentary (e.g. 'Unfortunately'), denying readers a guiding moral voice.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: matter-of-fact description with only minimal commentary

claims.claim: Töyrylä notes the Senzio courtyard slaughter is narrated in summary with 'according to most reports later' and approximate casualties, the narrator restricting omniscience to what becomes known.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: the narrator is merely reporting what happened, without any commentary

claims.claim: Töyrylä identifies a narrator who reports what the world seems like to an average inhabitant, adopting the Palm's religious stance ('as everyone knows') and using 'word went forth' to mislead truthfully.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: reporting what the world seems like to an average person

claims.claim: Töyrylä analyses tavern-patron and Astibar-town passages focalized through a group, combining sardonic tone with dramatic irony since readers know more.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: a sardonic tone is combined with the deeper level irony

claims.claim: Töyrylä argues Kay's 'outright lie' opening is not a lie: the narrator says only that word went forth of Sandre's death.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: the narrator does not claim that Sandre is dead

claims.feature: authorial aim: ambiguities and divided loyalties
claims.claim: Töyrylä quotes Kay's afterword that Tigana aimed to stretch the reader with ambiguities and divided loyalties in a genre that tends not to work that way.
claims.source: Roosa Töyrylä, 'Ambiguities and Divided Loyalties: Focalization in Guy Gavriel Kay's Tigana' (BA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2017)
claims.quote: to stretch the reader with ambiguities and divided loyalties

verdicts.trueWording: on a smaller scale and more obliquely expressed
verdicts.note: Cobb (Bright Weavings reprint, Foundation Summer 2005) raw text: Crispin 'receives and takes advantage of a new opportunity to realise something of his vision, on a smaller scale and more obliquely expressed'; next sentence: 'Because this work is on a smaller scale, it may actually last, and as Kay bases this mosaic project on mosaics yet surviving in Ravenna, the novel implies that they will last.' Quotation verbatim; every limb (second mosaic, smaller scale, oblique, novel implies it lasts) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the smallness of the human being in relation to the world
verdicts.note: Cobb raw text: 'Where Silverberg's protagonist sees himself as mastering history, Crispin sees his capacity to stand against history as much more modest... This sense of proportion, of the smallness of the human being in relation to the world, seems absent from Silverberg's story.' Quotation verbatim; contrast with the history-mastering hero explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: About sixty per cent of the text has Devin or Dianora
verdicts.note: Toyryla raw text (full thesis reprinted on Bright Weavings): 'About sixty per cent of the text has either Devin or Dianora as the focal character'; 'there are at least nineteen other focal characters that can be clearly identified'; 'most have at least three different perspectives alternating with each other.' All three limbs verbatim-supported.

verdicts.trueWording: incomplete sentences point in the direction of the character
verdicts.note: Raw text: 'the use of free indirect thought, or what Dorrit Cohn calls narrated monologue'; 'The metaphor of twin snakes is clearly hers, not the narrator's'; 'the deictic markers ("come here")... and the use of incomplete sentences point in the direction of the character as well'; Cohn's narrated monologue 'amplif[ies] the emotional notes' — 'obviously true... the above example included.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: The same goes for the long list of verbs
verdicts.note: Raw text: 'The same goes for the long list of verbs: "battered and levelled and burned . . . and killed . . . and taken away".' Framed by 'Dianora's own voice is allowed to come through in the passage' 'Despite being told in the narrator's voice'. Quotation and inner verb chain verbatim (ellipsis styling only differs).

verdicts.trueWording: Using the antagonist as a focal character makes him
verdicts.note: Raw text: 'one of the most regularly presented focal characters is Alberico'; 'Using the antagonist as a focal character makes him, however, a less distant figure than a commonplace dark lord'; 'Alberico may be a totally unsympathetic character, but he is nevertheless presented as a human being with human emotions like frustration and fear'; 'readers... are unlikely to sympathize with him.' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: some of the events are narrated twice or even thrice
verdicts.note: Raw text: the Ring Dive 'is focalized through both of them, and in addition Alessan, so that some of the events are narrated twice or even thrice, making the scene an instance of multiple focalization.' Contradictory readings present: Devin sees a face 'utterly expressionless. Icy cold' and judges it calculating; Dianora 'see[s] how ferociously he was struggling not to show what he was feeling'.

verdicts.trueWording: the focalization unexpectedly shifts to him
verdicts.note: Raw text: 'in the very last pages, the focalization unexpectedly shifts to him and it turns out that he is actually Valentin, the Prince of Tigana'; 'This plot twist is only achieved because Rhun does not appear as a focal character earlier in the book'; 'in the pivotal Ring Dive scene, all the focal characters pay some attention to Rhun.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: enables the matter-of-fact description of his execution
verdicts.note: Raw text: 'Ettocio is an innkeeper'; 'The latter part of the above excerpt shifts from Ettocio's perspective to narratorial focalization. This window shift distances the narration from Ettocio and enables the matter-of-fact description of his execution'; 'a minor character that is present in the text for only a few pages.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: matter-of-fact description with only minimal commentary
verdicts.note: Raw text: the ideological trace is 'essentially in the form of the word "unfortunately"' (novel excerpt reads 'Unfortunately, one evening in summer'); 'The narrator does not make strong moral judgments, denying readers the access to a guiding voice that would tell what is right or wrong. Instead, narratorial focalization often takes the form of matter-of-fact description with only minimal commentary.'

verdicts.trueWording: the narrator is merely reporting what happened, without any commentary
verdicts.note: Raw text on the Senzio castle-courtyard melee ('some thirty or forty Senzians'): 'the narrator is merely reporting what happened, without any commentary and in the summary fashion of ambient focalization'; the phrase 'according to most reports later'... 'suggests that the narrator is restricting their omniscience and narrating only what people hear about the incident afterwards'; 'The approximate number of the dead could also point in the same direction.'

verdicts.trueWording: reporting what the world seems like to an average person
verdicts.note: Raw text: 'instead reporting what the world seems like to an average person living in that world'; 'the narrator adopts the religious views of the people of the Palm' via 'as everyone knows'; and the opening 'word went forth' means 'the narrator does not claim that Sandre is dead... and that is the truth', 'while purposely misleading readers.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: a sardonic tone is combined with the deeper level irony
verdicts.note: Raw text: the tavern passage is 'not focalized through any single patron in the tavern, but instead collectively through the whole group of them'; the Astibar passage is 'the narrator briefly adopting the viewpoint of a group of people, this time the citizens of the town of Astibar'; 'a sardonic tone is combined with the deeper level irony... a kind of dramatic irony: a situation where readers know more than the characters.'

verdicts.trueWording: the narrator does not claim that Sandre is dead
verdicts.note: Raw text: 'Kay himself says in his afterword that he started the book with "an outright lie" (792), but that is not strictly speaking true since the narrator does not claim that Sandre is dead but states that such "word went forth", and that is the truth.' Quotation verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: to stretch the reader with ambiguities and divided loyalties
verdicts.note: Raw text: 'Kay himself writes in an afterword to his novel that one of his aims was "to stretch the reader with ambiguities and divided loyalties in a genre that tended (and still tends) not to work that way" (792)'. Quotation verbatim; afterword attribution and the genre limb both supported.
